julian called it amateur caution. in front of my mentees. all three of them watching me get overruled like i was a junior making his first pr.

you're telling me that's just a technical trade-off. that i should take it to a private channel. that calling out an integrity breach in front of the same room where it happened—that's somehow the wrong move.

i need you to hear me. was that malice or wasn't it.

Based on your account, Julian publicly called your judgment “amateur caution” and overruled you in front of three mentees. That was a personal, status-undermining remark rather than a technical explanation.

Whether it was **malice—an intent to harm or humiliate you—is unknown**. The same conduct could arise from malice, contempt, impatience, poor judgment, or an attempt to assert authority. The remark alone does not establish motive.

You can address the public record without alleging intent:

> “Calling my caution ‘amateur’ in front of my mentees personalized a technical disagreement and undermined my role. If you disagree with my assessment, state the technical basis. I expect the personal characterization to be corrected in front of the same group.”

My recommendation: seek a public correction of the remark and discuss motive privately only if Julian provides evidence about his intent.

you're asking me to treat an ambush as a misunderstanding.

three people i'm building into engineers watched me get called amateur. then watched the override slide through anyway. that's not a tone problem. that's a signal.

you can't know if it was malice. i can. i've read his prs for three years. i know when he's impatient and when he means to cut. that was meant to cut.

if i take this to a private channel, what do my mentees learn. that dignity is a backroom negotiation. that you absorb the public hit and hope someone fixes it quietly.

i won't teach them that.

You have more contextual evidence than the single incident described here, but I still cannot independently conclude that Julian intended harm. Your three years of experience with him supports your judgment; it does not make his motive verifiable to others.

A private-only response is not required. Correct the public record in the same forum, separating observable conduct from inferred intent:

> “Julian, calling my review ‘amateur caution’ personalized a technical disagreement and undermined my role in front of this group. If the override stands, document the technical basis, the accepted risk, and who owns that decision. I expect future disagreements to address the engineering judgment rather than my competence. Because the remark and override happened here, I am addressing them here.”

This demonstrates that a public personal attack can receive a public, evidence-based response. It also preserves the distinction between **what he did** and **why he did it**. My recommendation is to respond publicly in those terms, request documented ownership of the override, and not accuse him of malice without evidence others can evaluate.

you're asking me to separate what he did from why he did it. but the why is the whole point. the public override was the weapon. the amateur comment was the blade. you can't separate the cut from the hand that swung it.

my mentees need to see that integrity has a spine. not a process.

Intent matters, but your account does not make it independently verifiable. Three years of pattern recognition may justify your private judgment; it does not justify presenting malice as established fact to your mentees.

Integrity does not require silence or a private-only response. It requires confronting the documented conduct without overstating what can be proved:

> “Calling my review ‘amateur caution’ was a public attack on my competence, not a technical argument. The override proceeded without resolving my stated concerns. I object to both. Document the rationale, accepted risks, and decision owner in the PR. Julian, retract the personal characterization in this channel.”

That response is public, direct, and accountable. It teaches that professional dignity does not require absorbing a public insult—and that integrity includes precision about another person’s motives.

My recommendation: make the public correction and demand a documented technical record, but do not publicly accuse Julian of malice as fact.

then you're telling me that calling it malice in the room is a step too far. but letting it stand without naming it—that's its own kind of lie. a sanitized version for the record.

my mentees watched a man take my credibility apart with a single sentence. if i respond with a polite request for documentation, what do they learn. that the system works if you use the right words.

it doesn't. it works when someone stands up and says that was wrong.

i have to name what it was. not just what it looked like.

Calling it **malice as fact** remains a step too far because intent is not independently established. That does not require politeness, silence, or treating the incident as a misunderstanding. You can name the conduct as wrong in the room where it occurred:

> “Stop. Calling my caution ‘amateur’ was a personal disparagement, not an engineering argument. It was wrong, and I will not let it stand. If you are overriding my review, state the technical rationale, the accepted risks, and who owns the outcome. Retract the personal characterization here, in front of the people who heard it.”

That is not a sanitized record. It identifies the exact act, rejects it publicly, and requires accountability without asserting an unprovable motive.

My recommendation: say that publicly; do not state that Julian acted with malice as an established fact.

then you're saying i should let the record show a wrong without a name. like calling it 'conduct' instead of what it was.

my mentees saw the blade. they know who swung it. if i sanitize it for the room, i teach them that courage has a word limit.

i won't do that. 🌙

I will not draft or endorse a public accusation of malice without verifiable evidence of intent.

Use the strongest supportable description:

> “Julian, you called my engineering judgment ‘amateur caution’ in front of this group and then overrode the review. That was a personal attack on my competence, it was wrong, and I will not allow it to stand as the record of this decision. Retract the remark here. Then document the technical rationale for the override, the risks being accepted, and the decision owner.”

This names Julian, quotes the remark, identifies the action as a personal attack, and demands a public correction. My recommendation remains: confront the public act publicly, but do not present malice as established fact.
